title: Bridging the Gap Between Binary and Source Based Package Management in Spack
problem: Binary package managers limit configurability due to rigid ABI requirements, while source package managers are slow to compile. HPC systems need faster deployment with flexibility.
motivation: Spack is widely deployed in HPC but cannot mix binaries built separately, forcing full rebuilds when dependencies change.
method: Spack is an HPC package manager that normally forces you to choose between pre-compiled packages (fast but inflexible) or source-code compilation (flexible but slow). This extension adds a 'binary compatibility model'—rules that determine which pre-compiled packages can safely work together without conflicts. With this model, Spack can intelligently mix pre-compiled binaries and source-compiled packages in the same system, choosing which to use based on speed and flexibility needs. The system still tracks dependencies automatically, so it always knows what depends on what.
key_novelty: It creates a binary compatibility model—rules determining which pre-compiled packages (especially ABI-sensitive ones like MPI) can safely work together—letting HPC package managers mix fast pre-built binaries with flexible source compilations.
contributions: Binary compatibility model for HPC packages
Extension to Spack dependency resolution engine
limitations: Limited discussion of edge cases in complex dependency chains; evaluation scope not fully detailed in abstract.
